question: What will receiving financial advice in the future look like for clients?

claims.text: Position: personalization at scale, with the human relationship kept. Capgemini's World Wealth Report (published 2026-06-03) says the future of wealth management "will be defined by personalization at scale, underpinned by empathetic advisory relationships." It says life transitions, liquidity events and behavioral signals will increasingly decide when and how firms interact with clients, replacing calendar-driven review cycles with relevance-driven ones.

Position: trusted personal relationships stay central, helped by technology. On the 2Q26 earnings call (July 2026), Raymond James CEO Paul Shoukry said "the real value in this business has always been and always will be true personal relationships." He said that cannot be replicated by AI or technology "but it will be helped by AI and technology." He said the firm will keep investing in people, platforms and capabilities to help advisors deliver more holistic and personalized advice.

Position: advice stays a people business. On the 3Q26 call (October 2026), Morgan Stanley's CEO said that even if the technology is world-class, clients want to make decisions with their financial advisers based on the complexity of their own needs. He said technology can "do a lot of the early work."

Position: digital-first expectations and more acceptance of virtual advisor relationships. A Wealthtender advisor-search study (published 2025-08-13) says consumers now expect digital-first experiences even for traditional services like financial advice. Based on its data, it anticipates continued growth in AI tool usage for advisor searches. It also anticipates faster response expectations and further acceptance of virtual advisor relationships regardless of geographic location.

Position: competitive pressure from AI and robo-advice is reshaping delivery. The Edward Jones 2025 10-K (published 2026-03-13) says the industry has more firms providing personalized services and enhanced digital experiences, including AI and lower-cost computer-based "robo-advice." It says this has led, and is expected to keep leading, to significant investments in financial advisors, technology infrastructure, digital initiatives and data-powered tools. It also names changing client expectations and demographics, and generational wealth transfer, as risks to its ability to adapt its business model.

Position: advice-led, fee-based relationships as the destination for clients. On the 3Q26 call (October 2026), Morgan Stanley's CFO said clients either come in directly as fee-based accounts or migrate over time from self-directed. She said a little over 20% of all adviser-led flows are fee-based flows and that this "still holds, if not growing."

Position: AI augments advisors rather than replacing them. On the 2Q26 call (July 2026), Raymond James CEO Shoukry said the firm tells advisors: "AI will not replace advisers. Advisers who use AI will replace advisers who do not use AI." He said administrative time saved lets advisors spend more time on personal relationships. He said management believes the long-term ROI will exceed the cost of using AI.

Position: AI as "enhanced intelligence." On the 3Q25 call (published 2025-10-15), Bank of America CEO Brian Moynihan said the firm views AI as "enhanced intelligence, not an artificial intelligence," with teammates critical to delivering services. In the 2Q25 call (published 2025-07-16) he said AI helps relationship managers and advisors search and summarize information to prepare personalized planning and pitches.

Position: agentic AI could free up large amounts of advisor time. Deloitte (published 2026-05-20) says advisers spend nearly 70% of their time on behind-the-scenes work, leaving 30% for building client relationships. Its Center for Financial Services predicts adviser productivity uplift of roughly 30% to 100% by 2032. It says this could free between 25% and 50% of adviser time and potentially shift the issue from adviser scarcity to adviser capability.

Position: AI will transform advice, but most expect task automation. Accenture's survey (published 2025-06-23) found 97% say AI will have a transformative effect on the future of financial advice to a moderate or great extent in the next three years. 55% say AI will be most helpful in eliminating administrative tasks, identifying next best action opportunities, and automating marketing and client contact.

Position: AI will replace tasks, not the advisor, in core segments, though lower-touch models and younger clients may be different. McKinsey (published 2026-04-08) says the replacement thesis is "mostly false" for core advice segments, where nearly 80 percent of affluent households still prefer a human relationship. It says an AI takeover "might indeed be possible" for standardized, lower-touch service models and for younger clients, who are increasingly comfortable with AI-only interfaces.

Position: AI opens new distribution and more personal service. At Schwab on the 1Q26 call (published 2026-04-16), CEO Rick Wurster said "AI opens up new distribution channels and allows us to create personalized relationships with clients we have not been able to serve with a person-to-person relationship." Schwab's 3Q26 release (published 2026-10-15) says it introduced Charley, an AI-powered assistant giving U.S. retail clients conversational access to Schwab's tools and insights. It also partnered with Anthropic to bring Claude for Financial Advisors to the independent RIAs it serves.

Position: client comfort with AI is highest for monitoring and administrative tasks. A Wealthtender survey (published 2025-08-13, data snapshot from July 2025) found 77% comfortable with AI monitoring accounts for unusual activity. 74% were comfortable with AI analyzing market data to inform recommendations, and 74% with AI drafting routine client communications. The study says comfort with AI is lower for autonomous decision-making.

Position: AI and digital tools carry risks the firms themselves name. The Edward Jones 2025 10-K (published 2026-03-13) says that as it deploys new digital tools and client-facing technologies, its exposure to fraud risk is expected to increase. It also says use of AI may expose the firm to additional information security, legal and regulatory risk. The Raymond James FY2025 10-K (published 2025-11-25) says inadequate AI practices could produce inaccurate or biased output, and says AI could raise security and privacy risks.

Position: advisors will be expected to deliver more holistic and bespoke advice. On the 1Q26 call (published 2026-04-22), Raymond James CEO Shoukry said advisors "have been expected and will continue to be expected to provide more holistic and bespoke financial advice." He said this will require the firm to provide technology, where AI can help. Schwab's 2026 investor-day deck (published 2026-05-14) lists "growing demand for holistic advice" and "rising investor expectations for sophisticated, personalized solutions."

Position: demand for holistic advice is rising. McKinsey (published 2025-02-10) reports the share of investors seeking more holistic advice grew from 29 percent in 2018 to 52 percent in 2023. Capgemini (published 2026-06-03) reports 47% of HNWIs will consolidate more wealth with wealth management firms that provide integrated access to specialists. A Barclays commercial director quoted there says future relationship managers will need to move from reactive, product-centric interactions toward more intentional, coordinated engagement.

Position: next-generation clients want holistic planning and fee transparency. Fidelity's 2025 Investor Insights Study (published 2025-10-09) says wealthy Gen X, Y and Z investors are reshaping the advisor-client relationship with a focus on holistic financial planning and life goal achievement. These households seek transparency in advisor compensation and broader life guidance beyond investment management.

Position: clients will pay for human advice, and fee rates have held steady. McKinsey (published 2025-02-10) says almost 80 percent of surveyed affluent households would rather pay a premium of 50 basis points or more for human advice than use a customized digital advice service priced at about ten basis points. It cites PriceMetrix by McKinsey showing fee rates for $1.0 million to $1.5 million advisory relationships averaging approximately 104 basis points since 2019, after compression from 2013 to 2018.

Position: fee-based advice has room to grow at self-directed firms. On the 2Q26 call (published 2026-07-21), Schwab CEO Wurster said only 5% of Schwab retail households are in a fee-based advice solution and 31% of Schwab clients said they are willing to pay for advice. Cerulli (published 2026-04-09) says even among investors with under $100,000 in financial assets, just 34% say they are not willing to pay for advice. It says self-directed platforms need a path of least resistance from self-directed to advised.

Position: advisor roles may shift toward capability and relationships, and affiliation models are uncertain. Deloitte (published 2026-05-20) says AI could potentially shift the issue from adviser scarcity to adviser capability. On the 2Q26 call (July 2026), Raymond James's CEO said that whether AI could create convergence among affiliation options is a "potentially" and "interesting to see how that kind of evolves over time" question.

Edward Jones's own stated direction (2025 10-K, published 2026-03-13): the firm describes investing in initiatives such as Financial Planning Services, where clients receive a more personalized experience with additional planning capabilities. It also describes targeting High Net Worth clients, Workplace, and a new digital platform for Next Generation investors. The 10-K says it cannot reliably predict the timing or outcome of these initiatives.

Position: automation paired with professional oversight within advisor-led relationships. Merrill's press release (2026-09-15) announced Tax Efficient Transition and Dollar Cost Averaging services in its Investment Advisory Program. The release says they combine automation with professional portfolio oversight to help advisors implement personalized investment strategies at scale. Clients are directed to speak with their Merrill advisor about eligibility.

Position: advice tiered by client wealth segment. At its November 2025 investor day (published 2025-11-05), Bank of America's deck described a Wealth Continuum. It labels Mass Market (<$500K) as "investment tools" with a "predominantly digital experience." It labels Mass Affluent ($500K-$1MM) as "goals-based advice" with "guidance delivered at scale." It labels High Net Worth ($1MM-$10MM) as "dedicated advice and customizable solutions for complex needs." It reports $0.2T of client balances in the Mass Affluent tier.

Position: providers must engage mass-affluent prospects earlier. Cerulli (published 2026-03-25) says opportunities to engage new clients drop from 44% among the affluent under 30 to 24% among those in their 50s. 32% of affluent respondents prefer the same provider for investing and banking. Cerulli says future prospects will likely have several provider relationships before meeting wealth management minimums, and that providers must define what a premium experience entails.

Position: online and remote meetings are becoming normal. A Wealthtender study (published 2025-08-13) reports many people still want their advisor to be local but prefer meetings conducted online. It anticipates further acceptance of virtual advisor relationships regardless of geographic location.

Position: multiple channels funneling into advice. Morgan Stanley's 10-Q (published 2026-08-04) says Wealth Management supports clients through three channels: Advisor-Led, Self-Directed and Workplace. On the 2Q26 call (published 2026-07-15), its CFO said it is working on a referral model for those without an advice relationship, starting as early as financial education and with 401(k) assets. Schwab's CEO (2Q26 call, published 2026-07-21) said more retail clients seek holistic advice "delivered seamlessly on their terms through a combination of people and increasingly AI-enabled technology."

Edward Jones's own channels and segments (2025 10-K, published 2026-03-13): the firm says its branch model is designed to serve clients through deep, personal relationships and comprehensive advice and planning, with advisors located in the communities where clients live and work. It also describes a new digital platform focused on attracting and retaining Next Generation investors, and a Workplace initiative.

Position: broader access to products once limited to wealthier clients. Capgemini (published 2026-06-03) expects new fund structures, strategic partnerships and tokenized delivery to lower barriers. It says portfolio construction that once required very substantial minimum investments will become broadly accessible.

gaps.what: No firm discloses quantified adoption of virtual or remote advice delivery. The evidence on remote advice is survey-based (Wealthtender), not firm-reported.
gaps.suggested_source: Firm investor-day decks or earnings calls on virtual advice adoption; client-preference surveys with larger samples

gaps.what: The evidence contains forecasts and stated intentions from firms and research houses, not outcomes. It holds no single authoritative projection of how advice delivery and fees will change.
gaps.suggested_source: Industry studies with longitudinal fee and delivery-model data (for example PriceMetrix, Cerulli) and firm filings over time
